raw_response.overlap_rationale: Both Study A (Anand 2011) and Study B (Anand 2012) are companion ethnographic articles written by Nikhil Anand drawing on the exact same 22-month ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Mumbai between 2007 and 2010, supported by the identical four funders (Stanford University, Social Science Research Council, Wenner-Gren Foundation, and National Science Foundation). Both papers investigate the same Jogeshwari settlements in northern Mumbai—specifically Premnagar, Meghwadi, and Banjrekar Wadi—alongside the same Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (BMC) water supply department and ward offices. While Study A frames the broader technopolitics of 'hydraulic citizenship' and water pressure across Marathi-Hindu settlements and Muslim-majority Premnagar (highlighting the January 1995 cutoff rule, application documentation, councilor patronage, illegal connections, booster pumps, and revitalized wells), Study B explicitly cites Anand (2011) three times and zooms in on Premnagar's 'municipal disconnect' and abjection through the interactions of residents, plumbers, and BMC engineers. Both articles analyze the same legal/administrative barriers, infrastructure failures, informal/illegal tapping, booster pump usage, and return to subterranean bore wells, including shared testimony from the 2008 resident documentary 'Pyasa Premnagar' (Shaikh 2008) and near-verbatim passages describing Premnagar's return to neighborhood wells. Treating them as independent empirical studies in synthesis would double-count the same fieldwork site and sample.
raw_response.study_a_sample_and_data: 22 months of ethnographic fieldwork (2007–2010) in northern Mumbai settlements in Jogeshwari (Premnagar, Meghwadi, and Banjrekar Wadi) and BMC water supply department headquarters and ward offices; qualitative interviews and participant observation with settlers (e.g., Rane), party workers/councilors (e.g., Surve), hydraulic/maintenance engineers (e.g., Patkar, Kerkar), plus the resident documentary film Pyasa Premnagar (Shaikh 2008). No fixed quantitative N reported.
raw_response.study_b_sample_and_data: 22 months of ethnographic fieldwork (2007–2010) in northern Mumbai settlements in Jogeshwari (focusing on Premnagar in comparison with Meghwadi and Banjrekar Wadi) and BMC water department ward offices; qualitative interviews and participant observation with Premnagar residents (e.g., Asif, Salim), licensed/informal plumbers (e.g., Rafiq-bhai, Abdul, Ahmed), and municipal water engineers (e.g., Rane, Gupte), plus the resident documentary film Pyasa Premnagar (Shaikh 2008). No fixed quantitative N reported.
